description: We're Jacks of No Trades: a multidisciplinary team with no particular specialty and no intention of sticking to one. From code and science to design and storytelling, we believe the best ideas happen when nobody stays in their lane. Masters of none, but willing to try everything.
summary:
The whole of Earth shares one song. 

We built a website to make that song a reality and show earthly beauty because everyone deserves to experience it. We used data on precipitation, active fires, carbon monoxide, and nitrogen oxide where we extracted values from each image through provided scales. These estimated values remix music in real time!

The challenge beseeches us to translate sight into multisensory experience, so the map's beauty isn't limited to those who can see, and Immearth does just that — and more. The maps can be explored by keyboard, screen reader, or written description, so sight is not required! We implemented a computer vision system as well as a 3D spatial audio setup, allowing the sound to come from all directions, making you feel as if you are travelling the Earth, listening and immersed in everything around you. Through this extraordinary creative process, Immearth turns an isolated image into a multisensory journey.
details:
What Immearth Does and How It Works

Immearth is an accessible web experience that remixes one shared song using five NASA Earth Information Center visualizations: precipitation, active fires, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, and near-surface temperature.

Visitors can explore intact geographic maps, adjust layer visibility and opacity, and travel through an 8-column × 6-row regional grid. Each region produces a different musical interpretation. Written descriptions explain the science and the listening experience, so visitors do not need to rely on color perception or audio alone.

Our Python acquisition and analysis pipeline downloads official NASA images and compares each region’s pixels with the visualization’s published palette. It rejects unclassified colors, text, coastlines, antialiasing, and no-data regions rather than inventing quantities. The resulting associations are estimates derived from reviewed color-scale labels—not NASA-calibrated pixel measurements.

Each field has a distinct musical relationship:

  • Precipitation: separate rain and snow palettes influence restrained swells and rhythmic variations. Rain and snow are never treated as one gradient.
  • Active fires: sparse accents respond to estimated fire radiative power, not a fabricated fire count.
  • Carbon monoxide: nonuniform estimated CO palette tiers change the strength of a filtered branch of the music.
  • Nitrogen oxides: estimated values are mapped logarithmically to the recording’s spectral brightness.
  • Near-surface temperature: warmer estimated regions modestly increase the original recording’s playback speed.

All five fields modify “Deliberate Thought” by Kevin MacLeod, used under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0, with attribution preserved. There is one shared source, audio context, and musical clock. Filters, gain changes, envelopes, and playback-rate adjustments modify the existing recording rather than substituting generic beeps or unrelated generated sounds.

Interactive and Spatial Listening

Optional head-directed listening supports “look to preview, return to travel.”

Holding a direction previews a neighboring region’s musical interpretation and places the shared source artistically in that direction. Returning to center promptly commits one grid movement and returns the source to the listener-local origin. This lets people explore without repeatedly moving their mouse or losing their current map selection.

The browser’s generic spatial renderer produces directional sound using a single existing source. These listening coordinates are artistic local positions—not GPS measurements, calibrated geographical locations, or measured head movements. Headphones are recommended, but we do not claim guaranteed physical localization.

The camera remains off until explicitly enabled. Face-direction processing happens locally with MediaPipe; frames are not saved or uploaded. Spatial audio, head control, and playback all require separate opt-ins, and music never autoplays.

Benefits and Intended Impact

NASA visualizations communicate enormous amounts of environmental information, but those images can be inaccessible to people who cannot see the map or distinguish its colors. Immearth gives that imagery a voice and an explanation.

Its purpose is not to replace scientific analysis but to open a different way into Earth science:

  • Accessibility: keyboard operation, textual descriptions, regional summaries, optional voice navigation, and no mandatory audio or camera use.
  • Discovery: people can explore regional differences through familiar musical cues rather than inspecting dense scientific grids alone.
  • Comparison: five independent environmental fields can be explored on one geographic stage without suggesting that different quantities can be merged numerically.
  • Engagement: a restrained shared composition makes environmental patterns easier to notice and emotionally memorable without turning them into alarms or entertainment-only gimmicks.
  • Privacy: camera direction and voice processing stay local, with permission-dependent activation.
  • Scientific honesty: extracted scales remain clearly marked as estimates. Acquisition dates are distinguished from download timestamps, and an animation’s first frame is never described as the latest observation.

The intended impact is greater curiosity and inclusion around NASA Earth science. A teacher could use Immearth to introduce environmental patterns; a blind or low-vision visitor could navigate the map using sound, text, and input controls; and any visitor could gain a more memorable, personal connection with a field they may otherwise never explore.

We deliberately avoid suggesting that the project diagnoses weather events, predicts disasters, measures environmental harm, or produces literal sounds of pollutants.

Accessibility

Immearth works without sight, without hearing, and without a mouse. Controls are named in words; the chosen map says Chosen, and each move is announced as a region, row, column, and map. What the music is doing is written out, so the piece can be followed in silence.

A screen reader, a keyboard, and a mouse share the same controls. W, A, S, D, and the arrow keys move across the grid, and those keys stay quiet while you are on a button, link, or slider. Voice, the camera, and the music stay off until you ask. Dark mode, Color blind colors, and your own settings for motion, text size, and contrast are kept. A short tour stays until the last step.

Tools and Implementation

The application uses:

  • React 19 and Vite for the website.
  • JavaScript and the Web Audio API for shared audio transport, mixing, filtering, scheduling, and spatial rendering.
  • Python, Pillow, and NumPy for NASA image acquisition, geographic overlay preparation, palette comparison, and regional feature analysis.
  • MediaPipe for optional local coarse face-direction estimation.
  • An on-device keyword spotter for optional voice navigation.
  • DeepSpace for hosting the static site.

https://github.com/jjlols/Immearth

No special hardware is required. The website works on ordinary browsers, with headphones recommended for spatial listening.

Creativity and Curiosity as a Multisensory Framework

Our key creative choice was to use one composition shared across planet-scale scientific fields, rather than assigning each dataset an unrelated sound generator.

The world is visually connected, but scientific images are often encountered in isolation. Immearth places them in a shared musical environment. A person does not merely click a legend; they move through regions, hear differences, return to familiar territory, and form a relationship with the map.

Head-directed exploration adds a sense of presence and agency. The interface becomes less like a dashboard and more like a journey, while remaining grounded in bounded musical states rather than an overwhelming sound per pixel.

The central artistic idea is simple: the whole of Earth shares one song, and different people should be able to experience it in different ways.
